items.stem: Read an extract from a comedy, ‘Stage Fright’. ‘A school stage, the night of the play. Behind the curtain. OMAR, dressed as a tree, paces. OMAR: (to the audience) Twelve lines. I have twelve lines and I can remember precisely none of them. (Enter MRS CHEN, the director, with a clipboard.) MRS CHEN: Omar! Places, please. Two minutes. OMAR: Mrs Chen, I think I’ve got a fever. MRS CHEN: (feeling his forehead) You’ve got stage fright. Everybody has it. Even trees. (She exits. OMAR takes a deep breath and turns to face the curtain. It begins to rise.) OMAR: (whispering) Here goes.’ How does the playwright create comedy in this extract?
items.answer: Visual comedy of the tree costume; aside to the audience; exaggeration (precisely none); brisk dialogue; joke ‘Even trees’; curtain rising for a comic cliffhanger.

items.stem: Read an extract from a play, ‘The Clock’: ‘A cluttered attic. Evening. Rain against the window. JAMIE (14) kneels beside an open trunk. Enter TARA (16), holding a torch. TARA: What are you doing up here? JAMIE: (without turning) Nothing. TARA: That’s Grandad’s trunk. Mum said— JAMIE: I know what Mum said. (He lifts out a small brass clock. Its glass is cracked.) TARA: (quietly) You broke it. JAMIE: It was already like this! I just... wanted to see it. (Pause. TARA sits on the floor beside him. She takes the clock gently.) TARA: He used to wind it every Sunday. Said it was the only thing in the house that never lied. (Thunder. The torch flickers and goes out. Darkness.) JAMIE: Tara?’ Identify three conventions of a playscript used in this extract and explain how each helps a director or actor.
items.answer: E.g. setting description at the start (helps design the stage); character names before lines (shows who speaks); stage directions in brackets (how to move or speak, e.g. pauses, props, lighting); entrances and exits; sound or lighting cues.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 per convention correctly identified with an example; further marks for explaining its use in performance.

items.stem: Explain why playwrights include stage directions such as (quietly) or (without turning).
items.answer: They tell actors how to deliver lines and move, revealing feelings that the words alone may not show.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: guide performance; reveal emotion/subtext.

items.stem: Explain why playscripts do not use speech marks.
items.answer: Almost everything in a script is speech, and each speaker is shown by their name, so speech marks are unnecessary.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: names show the speaker; script is mainly dialogue.

items.stem: Turn this story extract into a short playscript: ‘Ines tapped her pen on the desk. “Tell me the truth,” she said quietly, “or don’t tell me anything.”’ Set it out correctly.
items.answer: Model: INES: (tapping her pen on the desk; quietly) Tell me the truth, or don’t tell me anything.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: names in capitals; no speech marks; stage directions in brackets in the present tense; meaning kept. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Turn this story extract into a short playscript: ‘“Where have you been?” asked Mum, folding her arms. Leo shrugged and dropped his bag. “Out,” he muttered.’ Set it out correctly.
items.answer: Model: MUM: (folding her arms) Where have you been? (LEO shrugs and drops his bag.) LEO: (muttering) Out.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for: names in capitals; no speech marks; stage directions in brackets in the present tense; meaning kept. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Write a scene about siblings clearing out their late grandmother’s house who find a hidden letter in which the characters want different things. Use an interruption to build dramatic tension at the key moment. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model approach: establish each character’s motivation early; escalate the conflict (grief, secrets and memory); place an interruption at the turning point; end with a resolution or a cliffhanger.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 7 marks, Style and accuracy 5 marks. Indicative content: clear, contrasting motivations; an interruption used at the turning point; rising tension; correct layout.

items.stem: Read ‘NADIA: (taking a deep breath) Because my mother worked here. For twenty years. Until you let her go.’ (an extract from a play, ‘The Interview’). Which language feature does the writer use here?
items.answer: Short sentence
items.markingKey: Short sentence: a deliberately brief sentence that stands out. Here ‘Until you let her go.’ – the short, blunt fragments build to an accusation that shifts power to Nadia.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘Even trees.’ in this line from an extract from a comedy, ‘Stage Fright’: ‘MRS CHEN: (feeling his forehead) You’ve got stage fright. Everybody has it. Even trees.’
items.answer: the comic short sentence releases tension with a joke.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘Even trees.’. Model point: the comic short sentence releases tension with a joke. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: You are directing an extract from a play, ‘The Clock’. Read this moment: ‘TARA: That’s Grandad’s trunk. Mum said— JAMIE: I know what Mum said.’ Explain how you would want the actors to perform it to show the characters’ motivation and build tension. Refer to voice, movement and timing.
items.answer: Interpretation: Jamie is defensive and irritated; he does not want to be reminded of the rule, which suggests guilt or strong emotion connected to Grandad. Performance ideas: tone of voice and volume, pauses before or after the line, eye contact or avoiding it, gestures with props, positioning on stage.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for a valid reading of motivation/tension; further marks for specific, justified performance choices (voice, movement, timing) linked to the text.

items.stem: Read ‘(Thunder. The torch flickers and goes out. Darkness.)’ from an extract from a play, ‘The Clock’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Pathetic fallacy (‘Thunder’): the storm and darkness reflect the characters’ grief and fear and create suspense.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (pathetic fallacy); 1 for selecting the key words ‘Thunder’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the storm and darkness reflect the characters’ grief and fear and create suspense.

items.stem: Read an extract from a play, ‘The Interview’: ‘A small office. A desk, two chairs. MS RAO, the manager, is typing. NADIA (17) stands in the doorway, clutching a folder. MS RAO: (not looking up) Sit. (NADIA sits on the edge of the chair. She drops the folder; papers scatter. She scrambles to collect them.) NADIA: Sorry. Sorry, I— MS RAO: Why do you want to work here? NADIA: (taking a deep breath) Because my mother worked here. For twenty years. Until you let her go. (MS RAO stops typing. A long silence.) MS RAO: (slowly) Does she know you’ve come? NADIA: No. (MS RAO closes the laptop.)’ Continue the scene after Ms Rao closes the laptop, showing how the balance of power between the two characters changes. Use playscript conventions. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: Ms Rao’s explanation or guilt; Nadia’s anger or doubt; pauses and interruptions; a final twist (a job offer, a secret about the mother).

items.stem: A script contains this stage direction: (He grips the back of the chair until his knuckles whiten.) Explain what it suggests to the audience about the character.
items.answer: The tight grip shows he is struggling to control anger or fear.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: a valid inference about the character’s feelings or situation linked to the action, e.g. the tight grip shows he is struggling to control anger or fear.

items.stem: Explain why stage directions in a script should be brief and in the present tense.
items.answer: They are instructions for performance happening now; brief directions are easy for actors to follow and leave room for interpretation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: present tense = live action; clarity/room for actors.

items.stem: Write the next six lines of this scene as a playscript, adding at least two stage directions. ‘Opening line: MOTHER: (staring at the clock) Ten years. Will we even recognise her?’
items.answer: Model continuation: the second character responds; a stage direction shows a reaction (e.g. (She turns away.)); the conflict escalates; a pause; a final line that leaves the scene open. Theme: anticipation and reunion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: correct layout; dialogue develops conflict; purposeful stage directions; consistent characters. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.
